prompt: Match each form of energy to an example.

right.text: A car driving along the road
A book on a high shelf

hints: Potential energies are stored. Kinetic energy is energy of movement.
solution: Kinetic → moving car. Gravitational potential → book up high. Elastic potential → stretched rubber band. Chemical → food. Sound → vibrating drum.

prompt: What is the unit of energy? (Give the name or the symbol.)
hints: It's named after the scientist James Joule.
solution: Energy is measured in **joules (J)**. 1 kJ = 1,000 J.

prompt: Food, petrol and batteries all store the same form of energy. What is it called?
hints: It's stored in the substances they are made of, and released by chemical reactions.
solution: **Chemical (potential) energy.** It is released by chemical reactions such as respiration in your cells or burning petrol.

prompt: Which of these is a **renewable** energy source?

options.text: Wind
Coal
Natural gas
Oil

feedback.b: Coal took millions of years to form and will run out, so it's non-renewable.
feedback.c: Natural gas is a fossil fuel, so it's non-renewable.
feedback.d: Oil is a fossil fuel, so it's non-renewable.

hints: Renewable sources are naturally replaced and won't run out.
solution: **Wind** keeps blowing and won't run out, so it is renewable. Coal, natural gas and oil are fossil fuels, which are non-renewable.

prompt: The law of conservation of energy says that energy cannot be [[a]] or destroyed. It can only be [[b]] from one form to another.
hints: The total amount of energy always stays the same.
solution: Energy cannot be **created** or destroyed. It can only be **transformed** from one form to another (or transferred from place to place).

prompt: A solar panel transforms [[a]] energy into [[b]] energy.
hints: What goes into a solar panel, and what comes out along the wires?
solution: A solar panel transforms **light** energy into **electrical** energy. Some of the energy is also wasted as heat.

prompt: Select **all** the renewable energy sources that are used to generate electricity in New Zealand.

options.text: Hydro (falling water)
Geothermal
Wind
Solar
Coal
Natural gas

hints: Two of the options are fossil fuels.
solution: **Hydro, geothermal, wind and solar** are renewable, and all are used in NZ. Hydro is the biggest source of our electricity. Coal and natural gas are non-renewable fossil fuels.

prompt: Match each type of heat transfer to an example.

right.text: A metal spoon in hot tea gets hot at the handle
Warm air rises from a heater and circulates around a room
You feel the Sun's warmth on your face

hints: Which method can cross empty space? Which one needs a fluid that can flow?
solution: Conduction → heat travels through the solid spoon. Convection → warm air rises and circulates. Radiation → infrared from the Sun crosses empty space.

prompt: Which type of heat transfer can travel through empty space, which is how the Sun's heat reaches Earth?
hints: Space is a vacuum, with no particles to pass the heat along.
solution: **Radiation** (infrared radiation). It needs no particles, so it can cross the vacuum of space.

prompt: Put the energy changes in a hydro power station in order, starting with the water in the lake.

items.text: Gravitational potential energy of water stored high in the lake
Kinetic energy of water rushing down the pipes
Kinetic energy of the spinning turbine

hints: The water starts high up and still. What does it have because of its height?
solution: Gravitational potential (water up high) → kinetic (falling water) → kinetic (turbine) → electrical (generator).

prompt: In every energy transformation, some energy is "wasted". What usually happens to it?

options.text: It becomes heat (thermal energy) that spreads out into the surroundings
It is destroyed
It is used up and disappears
It turns back into the original form of energy

feedback.b: Energy can never be destroyed. That's the law of conservation of energy.
feedback.c: Energy doesn't disappear. It changes into a less useful form.
feedback.d: It changes into a less useful form, usually heat, not back into the original form.

hints: Energy is conserved, so it must still exist somewhere. What form is it in?
solution: The wasted energy usually becomes **heat** (thermal energy), often caused by friction or electric currents. It spreads into the surroundings, so we can't use it. It isn't destroyed.

prompt: An electric motor is supplied with 800 J of electrical energy. It gives out 600 J of useful kinetic energy. What is its efficiency?
hints: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%.
solution: $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{600}{800} \times 100\% = 75\%$. The other 200 J is wasted as heat and sound.

prompt: A heater near the floor on one side of a room gradually warms the whole room. How does the heat get around the room?

options.text: Warm air becomes less dense and rises; cooler air sinks to replace it, making a convection current
Heat is conducted quickly through the air from particle to particle
Cold air rises because it is lighter
The heater pushes cold out of the room

feedback.b: Air is a poor conductor (an insulator), so conduction through air is very slow.
feedback.c: It's the other way round: warm air is less dense and rises.
feedback.d: Cold isn't a thing that moves. Heat flows from hot to cold.

hints: What happens to the density of air when it is heated?
solution: Air near the heater warms, expands, becomes **less dense** and **rises**. Cooler, denser air sinks and moves in to be heated. This **convection current** carries heat around the room.

prompt: A bungy jumper leaps from the Kawarau Bridge near Queenstown. At the very lowest point, when the cord is stretched as far as it goes, what form of energy is mainly stored in the cord?

options.text: Elastic potential energy
Kinetic energy
Gravitational potential energy
Chemical energy

feedback.b: At the lowest point the jumper stops for an instant, so there's almost no kinetic energy.
feedback.c: The jumper is at the lowest point, so gravitational potential energy is at its minimum.
feedback.d: Chemical energy is stored in food and fuels, not in a stretched cord.

hints: The cord is stretched. What kind of energy do stretched things store?
solution: The stretched cord stores **elastic potential energy**. The jumper's gravitational potential energy became kinetic energy during the fall, and then elastic energy in the cord. The cord then pulls the jumper back up.

prompt: Why do pots and pans often have handles made of wood or plastic?

options.text: Wood and plastic are poor conductors (insulators), so heat doesn't travel along them quickly
Wood and plastic are good conductors, so the heat escapes
Wood and plastic reflect heat radiation
Wood and plastic stop convection in the food

feedback.b: If they were good conductors, the handle would get hot and burn you.
feedback.c: The handle is protected mainly because heat can't conduct along it, not by reflection.
feedback.d: The handle has nothing to do with convection in the food.

hints: Heat travels along a solid handle by conduction.
solution: Wood and plastic are **insulators** (poor conductors), so heat conducts along them very slowly and the handle stays cool enough to hold.

prompt: An electric kettle is 85% efficient. It is supplied with 200 kJ of electrical energy. How much energy is wasted?
hints: 85% of the energy is useful. What percentage is wasted?
Find that percentage of 200 kJ.
solution: Useful energy $= 0.85 \times 200 = 170$ kJ. Wasted energy $= 200 - 170 = 30$ kJ (or 15% of 200 kJ). It is mostly lost as heat to the surroundings.

prompt:
A torch's batteries supply 100 J of energy. The bulb gives out 20 J of light.

Describe the energy transformations in the torch, say how much energy is wasted and in what form, and explain how this fits the law of conservation of energy.
modelAnswer: Chemical energy in the batteries is transformed into electrical energy, which the bulb transforms into light energy (useful) and heat (wasted). 100 − 20 = 80 J is wasted, mostly as heat. Energy is conserved because the total energy out (20 J of light + 80 J of heat) equals the 100 J put in. No energy was created or destroyed; most of it was just transformed into a form we didn't want.

rubric.criterion: Correct chain: chemical → electrical → light (+ heat)
80 J is wasted, mainly as heat (thermal energy)
Conservation: 20 J + 80 J = 100 J; energy is not created or destroyed, only transformed

hints: Where is the energy stored at the start?
If 20 J is light, where did the rest of the 100 J go?
solution: Chemical → electrical → light + heat. Wasted = 80 J (heat). Total out = 20 + 80 = 100 J = total in, so energy is conserved.

prompt: A vacuum flask keeps soup hot for hours. Why does the **vacuum** between its two walls reduce heat loss?

options.text: A vacuum has no particles, so heat can't pass through it by conduction or convection
A vacuum is very cold, so it keeps the soup cool
A vacuum reflects all infrared radiation
A vacuum sucks the heat back into the soup

feedback.b: A vacuum flask keeps hot things hot. A vacuum doesn't have a temperature of its own.
feedback.c: Radiation can cross a vacuum. The **shiny walls** reduce radiation.
feedback.d: A vacuum doesn't suck heat anywhere. It just has no particles to carry heat.

hints: Conduction and convection both need particles. What is a vacuum?
solution: Conduction and convection both need particles to carry the energy. A vacuum has **no particles**, so it blocks both. The shiny walls reflect radiation, and the stopper stops convection out of the top.

prompt: Select **all** the changes that would reduce heat loss from a house in winter.

options.text: Putting insulation in the ceiling
Installing double-glazed windows
Closing thick curtains at night
Leaving the windows open
Blocking draughts around doors
Replacing carpet with bare concrete floors

hints: Trapped air is a poor conductor.
Warm air escaping through gaps is convection.
solution: **Ceiling insulation, double glazing and thick curtains** all trap air, which is a poor conductor. **Blocking draughts** stops warm air escaping by convection. Open windows let warm air escape, and bare concrete conducts heat away faster than carpet.

prompt: Explain the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy sources. Give a New Zealand example of each, and describe one disadvantage of a renewable source.
modelAnswer: A renewable energy source is naturally replaced and won't run out, for example hydro power from the Waikato River, geothermal power at Wairākei, or wind. A non-renewable source took millions of years to form and will eventually run out, for example coal burned at Huntly Power Station or natural gas from Taranaki. A disadvantage of hydro is that it depends on rain: in a dry year the lakes get low and less electricity can be made. (Other examples: wind farms only work when the wind blows; dams flood land and change rivers.)

rubric.criterion: Renewable = naturally replaced / won't run out, with a valid NZ example (hydro, geothermal, wind, solar)
Non-renewable = will run out / took millions of years to form, with a valid example (coal, natural gas, oil)
A valid disadvantage of a named renewable source (e.g. hydro needs rain, wind is variable, dams affect rivers)

hints: Think about whether the source can run out.
Even renewable sources have problems. What happens to hydro in a drought?
solution: Renewable sources are replaced naturally (hydro, geothermal, wind, solar). Non-renewable sources will run out (coal, gas, oil). One disadvantage: hydro output drops in dry years, and wind only works when it's windy.

prompt: A ball is dropped and bounces. Each bounce is lower than the one before. What has happened to the energy?

options.text: Some is transformed into heat and sound at each bounce (and by air resistance), so less is left to lift the ball
Some energy is destroyed every time the ball hits the ground
The ball's gravitational potential energy is used up and disappears
The energy is stored in the ball and makes it heavier

feedback.b: Energy can't be destroyed. It is transformed into other forms.
feedback.c: It doesn't disappear. It turns into kinetic energy, then partly into heat and sound.

hints: What can you hear when the ball hits the ground?
Energy is always conserved.
solution: At each bounce some of the energy is transformed into **sound** and **heat** (in the ball, the ground and the air). Energy is conserved, but less of it is left as useful kinetic and gravitational potential energy, so each bounce is lower.

prompt: On a cold morning, a metal seat and a wooden seat in a park are at the **same** temperature. The metal seat feels much colder to sit on. Why?

options.text: Metal is a better conductor, so it carries heat away from your body faster
The metal is at a lower temperature than the wood
Metal lets cold flow into your body
Wood produces its own heat

feedback.b: The question says they are at the same temperature. Left outside overnight, they both cool to the air temperature.
feedback.c: Cold doesn't flow. Heat flows from your warm body into the colder seat.
feedback.d: Wood doesn't make heat. It is just a poor conductor.

hints: Heat flows from your warm body into the seat. Which material conducts heat better?
solution: Both seats are at the same temperature, but **metal is a good conductor**, so heat flows from your body into the metal much faster than into the wood (an insulator). You lose heat faster, so the metal **feels** colder.

prompt: Energy from the Sun ends up as electrical energy at a hydro power station. Explain the steps in how this happens.
modelAnswer: Energy from the Sun heats water in the sea, lakes and rivers, so some of it evaporates. The water vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as rain or snow on high ground. This water collects in a lake behind a dam, high up, so it has gravitational potential energy. When it flows down through pipes, this becomes kinetic energy, which turns the turbines. The generator transforms the turbines' kinetic energy into electrical energy.

rubric.criterion: The Sun's energy evaporates water, which later falls as rain (or snow) on high ground
Water stored high up in a lake / behind a dam has gravitational potential energy
Falling water's kinetic energy turns turbines, and the generator transforms this into electrical energy

hints: Think about the water cycle. How does water get up into the hills?
What form of energy does water have when it's stored high up?
solution: Sun → evaporation → rain in the hills → water stored high in lakes (gravitational potential energy) → falls through turbines (kinetic energy) → generator (electrical energy).

stem: Manapōuri Power Station in Fiordland is New Zealand's largest hydro power station. Water from Lake Manapōuri falls down pipes to turbines deep underground, then flows out through tunnels to the sea at Doubtful Sound.
prompt: As the water falls down the pipes, its [[a]] energy is transformed into [[b]] energy. The spinning turbines drive generators, which transform kinetic energy into [[c]] energy.
hints: Water stored high up has a kind of stored energy because of its height.
Anything that is moving has kinetic energy.
solution: Water high in the lake has **gravitational potential** energy. As it falls, this becomes **kinetic** energy. The turbines and generators transform the kinetic energy into **electrical** energy.

stem: Manapōuri Power Station in Fiordland is New Zealand's largest hydro power station. Water from Lake Manapōuri falls down pipes to turbines deep underground, then flows out through tunnels to the sea at Doubtful Sound.
prompt: The station is about 90% efficient. If some falling water supplies 4,000 kJ of energy, about how much electrical energy is produced from it?
hints: 90% efficient means 90% of the energy supplied ends up as useful electrical energy.
Find 90% of 4,000 kJ.
solution: Useful energy out = 90% of the energy in $= 0.9 \times 4000 =$ **3,600 kJ**. The other 400 kJ is wasted, mostly as heat.

stem: Manapōuri Power Station in Fiordland is New Zealand's largest hydro power station. Water from Lake Manapōuri falls down pipes to turbines deep underground, then flows out through tunnels to the sea at Doubtful Sound.
prompt: In a very dry year, the level of Lake Manapōuri falls. Why does this matter for the power station?

options.text: Less water is stored high up, so less gravitational potential energy is available
The water warms up, so it has less kinetic energy
Hydro power is non-renewable, so the water is running out forever
The turbines need rain to fall directly on them to make them spin

feedback.b: The water's temperature isn't the issue. What matters is how much water is stored high up, ready to fall.
feedback.c: Hydro is **renewable**: the lake refills when it rains. But in a dry year it may not refill fast enough.
feedback.d: The turbines are spun by water falling from the lake, not by rain landing on them.

hints: Where does the energy for a hydro station come from?
solution: A hydro station runs on the gravitational potential energy of water stored high in a lake. In a dry year less rain refills the lake, so there is **less stored energy** and less electricity can be generated. This is one disadvantage of relying on hydro power.

stem: Kiri does a bungy jump from a bridge near Queenstown. Measured from the lowest point of her jump, she has 30,000 J of gravitational potential energy as she stands on the bridge. At the lowest point she is still for a moment, and the stretched cord is storing 27,000 J of elastic potential energy.
prompt: Match each stage of the jump to its main energy transformation.

left.text: Falling, before the cord starts to stretch
Slowing down as the cord stretches
Bouncing back up as the cord shortens

right.text: Elastic potential → kinetic and gravitational potential

hints: When she speeds up, she is gaining kinetic energy. When the cord stretches, it is storing elastic potential energy.
solution: Falling: gravitational potential → kinetic. Cord stretching: kinetic → elastic potential (she slows down as the cord stores the energy). Bouncing back up: the cord's elastic potential energy → kinetic and gravitational potential energy.

stem: Kiri does a bungy jump from a bridge near Queenstown. Measured from the lowest point of her jump, she has 30,000 J of gravitational potential energy as she stands on the bridge. At the lowest point she is still for a moment, and the stretched cord is storing 27,000 J of elastic potential energy.
prompt: Only 27,000 J of the 30,000 J ends up stored in the cord. Explain what has happened to the other 3,000 J, and why this does **not** break the law of conservation of energy.
modelAnswer: The other 3,000 J has been transformed into heat (thermal energy) and a little sound, mainly because of air resistance as she fell and friction inside the stretching cord. This energy spreads out into the air and the cord, so it is "wasted". But it hasn't been destroyed: 27,000 J + 3,000 J = 30,000 J, the same total she started with. Energy has only been transformed into other forms.

rubric.criterion: The 3,000 J has been transformed into heat/thermal energy (and sound), e.g. by air resistance or friction in the cord
Conservation: the total is still 30,000 J (27,000 + 3,000); energy has been transformed, not destroyed

hints: What forces acted against her motion as she fell?
Add the useful and the wasted energy together.
solution: Wasted energy becomes heat (and sound). Useful + wasted = 27,000 J + 3,000 J = 30,000 J, so no energy was created or destroyed.

stem: Kiri does a bungy jump from a bridge near Queenstown. Measured from the lowest point of her jump, she has 30,000 J of gravitational potential energy as she stands on the bridge. At the lowest point she is still for a moment, and the stretched cord is storing 27,000 J of elastic potential energy.
prompt: What percentage of Kiri's starting gravitational potential energy is stored in the cord at the lowest point?
hints: Divide the energy stored in the cord by the energy she started with.
Multiply by 100 to get a percentage.
solution: $\dfrac{27\,000}{30\,000} \times 100 =$ **90%**. This is like the efficiency of the energy transfer from gravitational potential energy to elastic potential energy.

stem: Year 9 students go on a trip to some hot pools. The pools are filled with hot water from underground, and the air around them is cool.
prompt: Kiri lies on a deck chair beside the pool and feels the Sun's warmth on her skin, even though the air is cool. How does energy from the Sun reach her?

options.text: Radiation, which needs no particles to travel
Convection: warm air carries the heat from the Sun to her
Conduction: the heat passes from particle to particle through the air
Evaporation: steam from the pool carries the Sun's heat to her

feedback.b: Most of the distance between the Sun and Earth is empty space, with no air to make convection currents. And the air around her is cool.
feedback.c: Air is a poor conductor, and there are no particles in space to pass the energy along.
feedback.d: Steam from the pool carries the pool's heat, not the Sun's. The Sun's energy travels straight to her.

hints: There is empty space between the Sun and the Earth.
solution: The Sun's energy reaches her by **radiation** (infrared and light). Radiation doesn't need particles, so it can cross empty space, and it warms her skin even though the air is cool.

stem: Year 9 students go on a trip to some hot pools. The pools are filled with hot water from underground, and the air around them is cool.
prompt: When Kiri gets out of the pool she feels cold, so she wraps herself in a thick, dry towel. Why does the towel help to keep her warm?

options.text: It traps air, which is a poor conductor, so heat leaves her body more slowly
The towel gives out its own heat
The towel stops the cold from getting into her body
The towel reflects heat back to her like a mirror

feedback.b: A towel doesn't produce heat. It just slows down the heat leaving her body.
feedback.c: Cold isn't something that flows in. Heat flows **out** of her warm body into the cold air, and the towel slows this down.
feedback.d: A fluffy towel isn't shiny. It works mainly by trapping air, which is an insulator.

hints: Heat always flows from hot to cold. Which way is the heat flowing here?
solution: Heat flows from Kiri's warm body into the cold air. The towel's fibres trap lots of air, which is a poor conductor (an **insulator**) and can't move around much to carry heat away. So the towel slows down her heat loss.

stem: Year 9 students go on a trip to some hot pools. The pools are filled with hot water from underground, and the air around them is cool.
prompt: In one pool, hot water flows in near the bottom. Explain how the water at the top of the pool gets warm, even though the hot water enters at the bottom.
modelAnswer: The hot water entering near the bottom expands, so it is less dense than the cooler water around it, and it rises. Cooler, denser water near the top sinks down to take its place, and is then heated in turn. This movement forms a convection current, which carries heat around the whole pool, including the top.

rubric.criterion: Hot water expands / is less dense than the cooler water around it
So the hot water rises, and cooler, denser water sinks to replace it
This sets up a convection current that carries heat through the whole pool

hints: Think about how a heater near the floor warms a whole room.
What happens to the density of water when it is heated?
solution: Heating → less dense → rises; cooler water sinks → convection current → the whole pool warms up.

prompt: What form of energy does a moving object have?

options.text: Kinetic energy
Gravitational potential energy
Chemical energy
Nuclear energy

feedback.b: Gravitational potential energy is stored in an object because it is high up, not because it is moving.
feedback.c: Chemical energy is stored in substances such as food and fuel.
feedback.d: Nuclear energy is stored in the nucleus of atoms.

hints: The word comes from a Greek word meaning 'to move'.
solution: Every moving object has **kinetic energy**. The faster it moves (and the bigger its mass), the more kinetic energy it has.

prompt: What word describes energy sources, such as wind and hydro, that are naturally replaced and will not run out?
hints: The word means they can be 'made new' again.
solution: **Renewable** sources, such as hydro, geothermal, wind and solar, are naturally replaced. Coal, oil and natural gas are non-renewable.

prompt: Which type of heat transfer happens mainly in **solids**, as particles vibrate and pass energy on to their neighbours?

options.text: Conduction
Convection
Radiation
Evaporation

feedback.b: Convection needs a fluid (a liquid or a gas) that can flow.
feedback.c: Radiation doesn't need particles at all.
feedback.d: Evaporation is a change of state, not one of the three types of heat transfer.

hints: Think of a metal spoon getting hot in a cup of tea.
solution: **Conduction**: particles in a solid vibrate more when heated and pass the energy on to their neighbours. Metals are especially good conductors.

prompt: Select **all** the forms of **stored** (potential) energy.

options.text: Gravitational potential energy
Elastic potential energy
Chemical energy
Nuclear energy
Kinetic energy
Sound energy
Light energy

hints: Stored energy is waiting to be used, for example in a battery, a stretched rubber band or a book on a high shelf.
solution: Stored energies: gravitational potential (high up), elastic potential (stretched or squashed), chemical (food, fuel, batteries) and nuclear (in atoms). Kinetic, sound and light energy are energy on the move.

prompt: A wind turbine transforms [[a]] energy into electrical energy. A speaker transforms electrical energy into [[b]] energy.
hints: Wind is moving air.
What does a speaker produce for you to hear?
solution: Wind turbine: the **kinetic** energy of moving air → electrical energy. Speaker: electrical → **sound** energy (plus a little wasted heat).

prompt: An old-style light bulb is supplied with 60 J of electrical energy. It gives out 3 J of light. What is its efficiency?
hints: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100.
solution: Efficiency $= \dfrac{3}{60} \times 100 =$ **5%**. The other 57 J becomes heat, which is why these bulbs get so hot and why much more efficient LED bulbs have replaced them.

prompt: Which energy-flow diagram is correct for a petrol car engine?

options.text: Chemical → kinetic + heat + sound
Electrical → kinetic + heat
Kinetic → chemical + heat + sound
Chemical → kinetic

feedback.b: A petrol car gets its energy from burning fuel, which stores chemical energy, not from electricity.
feedback.c: This is backwards: the energy stored in the fuel is what makes the car move.
feedback.d: Some energy is always wasted, mainly as heat (and some sound), so the diagram should show it.

hints: Start with the energy stored in the petrol, and remember the wasted energy.
solution: Petrol stores **chemical** energy. The engine transforms it into **kinetic** energy (useful) plus heat and sound (wasted). Real energy-flow diagrams should always show the wasted energy.

prompt: Sam charges his phone with a small solar charger, then uses the phone to play music. Put the energy forms in order, starting with the energy from the Sun.

items.text: Electrical energy from the solar panel
Chemical energy stored in the phone's battery
Electrical energy flowing to the phone's speaker

hints: The solar panel makes electricity, but the phone stores it until it is needed.
Batteries store energy in chemical form.
solution: Light → electrical (solar panel) → chemical (stored in the battery) → electrical (when the phone is used) → sound (speaker). Some energy is wasted as heat at each step.

prompt: Wairākei Power Station near Taupō is a **geothermal** power station. Where does its energy come from?

options.text: Heat from hot rocks underground, which makes steam that spins the turbines
Burning natural gas from Taranaki to boil water
Water falling from Lake Taupō to spin the turbines
Wind blowing across the volcanic plateau to spin the turbines

feedback.b: Burning gas would make it a fossil-fuel power station. Geothermal stations use heat from the Earth itself.
feedback.c: That is how a hydro power station works.
feedback.d: That is how a wind farm works.

hints: 'Geo' means Earth and 'thermal' means heat.
solution: Geothermal stations use **heat from inside the Earth**. Hot water and steam from deep wells spin turbines connected to generators: thermal → kinetic → electrical. Wairākei was one of the first large geothermal power stations in the world.

prompt: What is the name for materials such as wool, polystyrene and air, which are poor conductors of heat?
hints: These materials are used to keep heat in, for example in a house's ceiling.
solution: Poor conductors of heat are called **insulators**. They slow down heat transfer, which is why they are used in ceilings, jerseys and chilly bins.

prompt: A toaster is supplied with 1,200 J of electrical energy. 900 J of heat goes into the bread to toast it. The rest heats the toaster itself and the air around it. How much energy is wasted?
hints: For a toaster, the heat that goes into the bread is the **useful** energy.
Wasted energy = total energy in − useful energy out.
solution: Wasted energy $= 1200 - 900 =$ **300 J**. For a toaster, heat is the useful output, so only the heat that doesn't go into the bread is wasted.

prompt: A double-glazed window has two panes of glass, with a narrow sealed gap of air (or another gas) between them. Explain why it reduces heat loss from a house compared with a single pane of glass.
modelAnswer: The sealed gap between the panes is filled with air (or another gas), which is a very poor conductor of heat. So much less heat is conducted from the warm inside pane to the cold outside pane than through a single sheet of glass. Because the gap is narrow and sealed, the air can't circulate much, so convection currents can't carry much heat across either. So less heat escapes through the window.

rubric.criterion: There is a layer of air (or gas) trapped between the two panes
Air is a poor conductor (an insulator), so less heat is conducted through the window
The gap is narrow and sealed, so convection is reduced too

hints: What is in the gap between the panes? Is it a good or a poor conductor?
Can the trapped air move around much?
solution: Double glazing works because the trapped layer of air (or gas) is an insulator, and the narrow sealed gap stops it moving around, which reduces both conduction and convection.

prompt: On a hot, sunny day, the inside of a black car gets hotter than the inside of a white car parked next to it. Why?

options.text: Dark surfaces absorb more of the Sun's radiation; white surfaces reflect more of it
Black paint is a better conductor of heat than white paint
Black cars attract heat, like a magnet attracts iron
White surfaces give out cold radiation, which cools the car

feedback.b: The difference is about how much of the Sun's radiation is absorbed, not how well the paint conducts.
feedback.c: Heat isn't attracted. The black car absorbs more of the radiation that falls on it.
feedback.d: There is no such thing as 'cold radiation'. White surfaces simply reflect more of the Sun's radiation.

hints: Think about what dark and light surfaces do with radiation that hits them.
solution: Dark, dull surfaces are good **absorbers** of radiation, while white, shiny surfaces **reflect** most of it. The black car absorbs more of the Sun's energy, so it gets hotter.

prompt: Most of New Zealand's electricity comes from hydro power stations. Explain why, in a very dry year, power companies may need to burn more coal or gas at Huntly Power Station.
modelAnswer: Hydro stations depend on rain (and melting snow) to keep their lakes full. In a very dry year the lake levels fall, so less water is stored high up, there is less gravitational potential energy available, and less electricity can be generated. Coal and gas can be stored and burned whenever they are needed, so Huntly Power Station can be used to make up the shortfall, although burning them releases more carbon dioxide.

rubric.criterion: Hydro depends on rain to refill the lakes
In a dry year the lake levels are low, so less water (energy) is stored and less electricity can be made
Coal and gas can be stored and burned whenever needed, so they make up the shortfall (with a cost, e.g. more carbon dioxide)

hints: What do hydro lakes need in order to stay full?
What is the advantage of a fuel that can be stored in a pile or a tank?
solution: Hydro relies on rainfall, which varies from year to year. Fossil fuels can be stored and used on demand, so they act as a back-up in dry years, but they add to climate change.

prompt: The 'wasted' heat from a car engine is not destroyed, but it can't easily be used again. Why not?

options.text: It spreads out into the surroundings, so it is too spread out and cool to be useful
It turns into cold, which cancels it out
It is changed into mass, which can't be used as energy
It flows back into the petrol tank as chemical energy

feedback.b: 'Cold' is not a form of energy. Something cold just has less thermal energy.
feedback.c: In a car engine, energy isn't turned into mass. It is transformed into other forms, mostly heat.
feedback.d: Energy doesn't flow back into the fuel. Burning fuel is a one-way process.

hints: Think about what happens to the heat from a hot engine on a cold day.
solution: Energy is conserved, but the wasted heat **spreads out** into the air and the road. It warms a huge amount of air by a tiny amount, so it is too spread out (and too cool) to do anything useful. That's what 'wasted' really means.

prompt: An electric kettle is 80% efficient. To boil some water, 160 kJ of energy must go into the water. How much electrical energy must be supplied to the kettle?
hints: 80% of the energy supplied ends up in the water.
So 160 kJ is 80% of the energy supplied. What is 100%?
solution: Useful energy = 80% of the energy supplied, so energy supplied $= \dfrac{160}{0.8} =$ **200 kJ**. Check: 80% of 200 kJ is 160 kJ, and the other 40 kJ is wasted heating the kettle and the air.
